thesis: This episode argues that successful game companies eventually evolve into platform-based publishers that own stakes in other studios and build 'forever games,' whereas those that treat games as a secondary revenue stream or fail to adopt this model ultimately struggle. It contrasts the long-term success of Tencent and Riot with the failures of Facebook, Discord, and Google to become sustainable customer acquisition vehicles for the gaming industry.

claims.claim: Tencent was successful because they embraced being a platform-based publisher, owned stakes in Epic and Riot, and invested deeply in games.
claims.quote: My opinion is that, why QQ was successful was that they didn't just decide that they're going to be a platform-based publisher. They embraced being a platform based publisher. They went out and did deals. They own 49% of Epic. They owned 51% of Riot, now 100% of Riot.

claims.claim: Facebook treated games as a bad smell, flirted briefly with Zynga, but ultimately failed to become a customer acquisition vehicle for the games industry.
claims.quote: Instead of Facebook or some of these other American platforms that have treated games as a bad smell over in the corner that they weren't too crazy about, okay, yeah, the Zynga thing they flirted with briefly, but ultimately, that didn't go that well.
